props.title: The Kingmaker

sections.content: Lauren Greenfield's **The Kingmaker (2019)** (2019) offers a chilling portrait of Imelda Marcos, examining how power corrupts and history gets rewritten by its victors. Like Joshua Oppenheimer's The Act of Killing (2012), it gives its subject enough rope to reveal their true nature. Marcos's attempts to rehabilitate her family's image and engineer her son's political rise unfold with the same unsettling intimacy found in The Queen of Versailles (2012), another Greenfield film about wealth's corrupting influence.

sections.content: The film's exploration of historical revisionism connects strongly to other political documentaries like **The World Before Her** (2012) and **The Look of Silence** (2014). Greenfield captures how Marcos weaponizes nostalgia for the dictatorship years, paralleling themes in **The Last Emperor** (1987) about how rulers craft their own mythology. The director's access to Marcos reveals both calculated performance and unguarded moments of shocking candor about wealth, power, and entitlement.

Like **Five Came Back** (2017) and The Fog of War (2003), **The Kingmaker** demonstrates how documentary can interrogate history through personal testimony. The film's examination of the Marcos family's continued influence in Filipino politics echoes Get Me Roger Stone (2017) in showing how political operatives maintain power through manipulation of media and public perception. sections.content: Greenfield's approach recalls the work of Claude Lanzmann in **Shoah** (1985), allowing subjects to reveal themselves through extended interviews while carefully contextualizing their claims. The film's exploration of the Marcos family's stolen wealth and extravagant lifestyle connects to themes in **Inside Job** (2010) and **All the Queen's Men** (2019), showing how political corruption enables massive personal enrichment.
